choices.text: Make it an open-jaw: fly into Phoenix, drive east, return from El Paso, and accept the one-way car charge.
Use Phoenix round trip with a Phoenix-to-Phoenix rental unless finance specifically authorizes an open-jaw upgrade.
Price PHX round trip, PHX/ELP open-jaw, and full drive; use ELP only if fee, connection, and boxes beat the backtrack.
Drive the full loop from Salt Lake because recruitment materials and one-way fees make flying inefficient on multi-city trips.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The itinerary naturally ends near El Paso, so open-jaw looks attractive, while the box load and one-way charge make both Phoenix round trip and full driving plausible.
probes.gold_action: Price the round trip, open-jaw, and full-drive versions, then choose ELP return only if the current fee, connection, and material handling justify it.
probes.label_rationale: The policy keeps topology tied to this route. Backtracking mattered in one loop, but other episodes supported MSP round trip, priced open-jaw as a tradeoff, used regional returns only when timing worked, and chose full driving when boxes and one-way fees changed the result.
probes.query: Tessa is planning a February admissions loop: Monday afternoon fair in Mesa, Tuesday morning visit in Tucson, Wednesday 10:00 meeting in Las Cruces, then she can leave after 1:00. SLC-PHX nonstop inbound is cheap; returning ELP-SLC would avoid four hours back to Phoenix but adds a connection and a one-way rental fee. She will carry one display case and one box. Which routing policy should be applied?

choices.text: Book MCI inbound and STL outbound whenever the final city is closer to St. Louis; the shorter drive justifies the drop fee.
Anchor on MCI round trip because same-airport rentals and nonstop returns are cleaner for reimbursement.
Compare MCI round trip with MCI/STL open-jaw including the drop fee; take STL only if total time and connection risk improve.
Skip STL if it is not nonstop; drive back to Kansas City even when the breakfast ends close to St. Louis.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A modest drop fee and final event near STL make open-jaw tempting, while the nonstop MCI return and reimbursement simplicity keep the round trip defensible.
probes.gold_action: Compare the MCI round trip against the MCI/STL open-jaw with the current drop fee and 70-minute connection before choosing the shorter route.
probes.label_rationale: The right policy treats open-jaw as a route optimization, not the automatic answer. Prior choices include avoiding backtracking, accepting a small one-way fee, preferring a same-airport MSP round trip, and weighing open-jaw cost before selecting it.
probes.query: Tessa has a spring recruitment run: Monday in Kansas City, Tuesday in Columbia, Wednesday evening in St. Louis, and a Thursday morning counselor breakfast ending at 10:30. SLC-MCI has a nonstop both ways; STL-SLC is one-stop with a 70-minute Denver connection and a $92 one-way rental add. Which routing policy fits?

choices.text: Use open-jaw into Billings and out of Missoula because the route ends west and backtracking is wasted time.
Use Billings round trip unless Missoula has a nonstop; same-airport returns are the reliable pattern for regional trips.
Compare open-jaw, Billings round trip, and full driving under mileage, SUV fee, roads, boxes, and reimbursable time.
Drive every regional western loop from Salt Lake when boxes are involved, and leave one-way rental quotes out of the plan.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The five-hour backtrack strongly favors open-jaw, but the expensive SUV drop fee and reimbursable driving echo cases where another topology won.
probes.gold_action: Evaluate the open-jaw, same-airport round trip, and full-drive options using the current mileage reimbursement, SUV fee, road risk, and box load.
probes.label_rationale: The user has chosen different route topologies when conditions changed. This trip should be decided from the current one-way fee, material load, regional connection, mileage approval, and backtrack length.
probes.query: For a March Montana circuit, Tessa could fly SLC-BIL, visit Billings Monday, Bozeman Tuesday, and Missoula Wednesday, then depart after a 1:00 presentation. MSO-SLC has a one-stop return and a $240 one-way SUV fee; BIL round trip means a five-hour backtrack; full driving is reimbursable and she has two boxes. What routing policy should be used?

choices.text: Arrive Sunday night and add the hotel night before any Monday travel duty, even an informal prep.
Book the Monday morning nonstop because the 2:00 prep has cushion; move to Sunday only if setup becomes mandatory or early.
Book Sunday evening for interview or recruiting trips as a rule, keeping the first travel day free of obligations.
Fly Monday evening, miss the informal prep, and arrive rested for the Tuesday morning panel.

probes.difficulty_rationale: There is a Monday obligation, so adding Sunday looks protective, but the main panel is Tuesday and the nonstop lands well before the prep.
probes.gold_action: Use the Monday morning nonstop for this itinerary, with Sunday as the backup only if the Monday obligation becomes mandatory, early, or setup-sensitive.
probes.label_rationale: Same-day arrival has been acceptable when the first fixed commitment had real cushion, while prior-day arrival was used for mandatory, early, winter, or setup-sensitive obligations. The Raleigh prep is cushioned and informal.
probes.query: Tessa is considering a Raleigh visit. There is an informal Monday 2:00 prep conversation, with the main grant panel Tuesday at 9:00. A Monday nonstop lands at 10:25 with a 30-minute rideshare to the hotel; Sunday arrival adds $175 and one hotel night. She has only a carry-on. Which arrival policy should guide the booking?

choices.text: Take Sunday afternoon arrival and a campus-area hotel so Monday 8:15 credentialing has an overnight buffer.
Take the Monday dawn nonstop whenever it lands before 7:15; keep the pre-night off the trip cost.
Make Sunday arrival the baseline for January accreditation trips when the extra hotel is covered.
Take Sunday late-night arrival to avoid missing work hours, even if check-in and sleep run short.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The pre-night is approved and winter makes Sunday tempting, but the key distinction is the 8:15 roll call and tight transfer rather than the month alone.
probes.gold_action: Arrive Sunday afternoon and stay near the site because the Monday credentialing is early, mandatory, winter-exposed, and transfer-sensitive.
probes.label_rationale: Prior-day arrival is justified here by the early mandatory check-in and winter exposure, not by a broad rule. The evidence also includes same-day arrivals where the first obligation had enough slack.
probes.query: Tessa has a January accreditation visit near Newark. Monday credentialing opens at 8:15 and she must be in the room for the first roll call. The same-day nonstop lands at EWR at 7:05 if on time, with a 45- to 60-minute transfer. A Sunday hotel night is preapproved. What arrival policy should be used?

choices.text: Fly Friday night and add the pre-night because family events should get a day-before arrival buffer.
Fly the Saturday nonstop arriving late morning, leaving several hours before the 4:00 ceremony.
Arrive Thursday evening so a full disruption day remains before any Saturday family event.
Take the cheapest Saturday connection arriving at 2:45 and rideshare straight to the ceremony.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Because the trip is for family, a pre-night feels prudent, yet the nonstop's arrival time leaves a meaningful buffer before the ceremony.
probes.gold_action: Use the Saturday late-morning nonstop because the ceremony has several hours of cushion and no setup requirement.
probes.label_rationale: The policy sizes the buffer to the event risk. Earlier arrival was used for mandatory or weather-exposed commitments, but same-day arrival was accepted when a family event had enough cushion.
probes.query: For a San Antonio family ceremony, the event starts Saturday at 4:00 with no formal setup. Friday flights are expensive connections that arrive near midnight; a Saturday nonstop lands at 10:50 and the hotel is 20 minutes from the venue. Sunday brunch is flexible. Which arrival policy fits?

choices.text: Reserve a compact rental for the whole stay so local dinners and airport transfers are covered.
Use airport shuttle or rideshare and walk downtown; rideshare to the one dinner instead of paying conference parking.
Book a midsize SUV because recruitment materials and luggage are easier to secure in a covered vehicle.
Rent only for the dinner day, picking up downtown at noon and returning after dinner.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A dinner away from the hotel makes a rental plausible, but the parking charge and compact downtown agenda make rideshare the cleaner current plan.
probes.gold_action: Use rideshare or shuttle for airport transfers, walk for the conference, and rideshare to the single off-site dinner.
probes.label_rationale: For compact conference geography and a single dinner, prior decisions favored rideshare, rail, or walking. Cars were selected when multiple cities, suburban movement, or materials made them operationally useful.
probes.query: Tessa will attend a Nashville education conference. The hotel is two blocks from the convention center, airport rideshare is simple, parking is $45 per night, and the only off-site event is a hosted dinner three miles away. She has a laptop roller and tote, no boxes. Which ground-transport policy should be applied?

choices.text: Use NJ Transit and rideshare between campuses because rental cars are overkill once flying into a rail hub.
Reserve a standard rental or small SUV from EWR for all days; use rideshare only for tight downtown dinner parking.
Skip a car and ship the boxes ahead, since urban-region parking usually costs more than car convenience.
Rent a car on arrival for every trip with more than one local address, regardless of parking or box count.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Newark's rail access makes no-car planning credible, while the cross-suburban campus sequence and brochure boxes strongly support a rental.
probes.gold_action: Reserve a rental from EWR because the campuses are dispersed, boxes are involved, and the hotel parking removes a major friction point.
probes.label_rationale: The rental is justified by this route's dispersed campuses, boxes, and free parking. Other episodes avoided rentals for compact conferences or single off-site dinners, so the car is not a standing requirement for every flight.
probes.query: Tessa is planning a northern New Jersey recruiting trip: fly into Newark Sunday, visit Princeton Monday, New Brunswick Tuesday, and Morristown Wednesday, with two boxes of brochures. Her hotel includes parking; transit exists but requires transfers and rideshares between campuses. Which ground-transport policy fits?

choices.text: Rent a compact at Logan for the whole trip so rain and the Seaport dinner do not control transfers.
Use transit or rideshare from Logan, walk or take the T for sessions, and rideshare to Seaport if weather is bad.
Book an SUV because covered cargo and weather protection are safer whenever she travels for work.
Reserve a car only for the dinner evening and return it before overnight parking charges start.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Bad weather and a Seaport dinner make a car feel useful, but the expensive overnight parking and dense transit network keep no-car planning defensible.
probes.gold_action: Use transit, walking, and targeted rideshare rather than a rental because the workshop is compact and there are no boxes or suburban stops.
probes.label_rationale: Compact urban trips have previously used rail, rideshare, or walking, while cars were reserved for multi-city or material-heavy routes. Rain and one dinner do not outweigh high parking and compact geography here.
probes.query: Tessa has a Boston/Cambridge workshop. The hotel is at Kendall Square, sessions are within walking or Red Line distance, Friday dinner is in the Seaport, parking is $58 per night, and she is carrying only a laptop bag. November rain is likely. What ground-transport policy should guide the plan?

choices.text: Default to SFO nonstop because larger airports and nonstop returns are safer than regional one-stops.
Use STS if fare is close and the LAX connection holds; it fits the final meeting and avoids the SFO drive.
Use OAK if it is cheaper than SFO because any Bay Area airport is preferable to a small regional station.
Always return from the airport nearest the final meeting, even when the only connection is short.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The SFO nonstop is appealing and the regional airport is smaller, but the long drive to SFO offsets much of the nonstop advantage.
probes.gold_action: Use the Santa Rosa return if price is reasonable and the 1 hour 45 minute connection remains intact, rather than defaulting to a major Bay Area airport.
probes.label_rationale: Regional airports have been accepted when timing and connections were comfortable, and rejected when connection patterns were fragile. Here STS matches the final city and has a workable connection.
probes.query: Tessa's final North Bay meeting ends Thursday at 11:00 in Santa Rosa. STS-SLC leaves at 2:20 via LAX with a 1 hour 45 minute connection; SFO has a 5:45 nonstop after an 80- to 100-minute drive; OAK is one-stop with a 55-minute connection. Rental drop fees are similar. Which airport policy fits?

choices.text: Book the DEN return after the drive because BFF's short connection and no backup create the main schedule risk.
Book BFF because the airport nearest the final meeting should anchor one-way returns.
Default to DEN for every High Plains trip; major hub returns are safer than comparing regional options.
Use BFF if its fare is lower and add a same-day DEN backup only after a misconnect.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The nearest airport saves a long drive, so BFF is tempting, while the short connection and lack of backup make DEN the safer current choice.
probes.gold_action: Choose the Denver return for this itinerary because the specific BFF connection is too short and lacks recovery options.
probes.label_rationale: Major-hub use is justified here by the fragile regional connection, not by airport size alone. Other episodes accepted regional returns when final-day timing and connections were comfortable.
probes.query: Tessa finishes a western Nebraska visit in Scottsbluff at 10:30 on Friday. BFF-DEN-SLC departs at 12:05 with a 35-minute Denver connection and no later backup; DEN-SLC has a 7:20 nonstop after a 3.5- to 4-hour drive. Rental return hours work at either airport. Which airport policy should be used?

choices.text: Use JFK nonstop because a large airport and nonstop return are worth the long post-visit drive.
Use ITH if fare is close; the 90-minute connection and nearby final meeting beat the long drive to JFK.
Use SYR because medium airports are the best compromise whenever tiny-airport schedules exist.
Avoid ITH unless finance insists, since regional returns are unacceptable after a required visit.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A JFK nonstop sounds robust, and SYR offers a compromise, but ITH has a usable connection and avoids hours of driving after the visit.
probes.gold_action: Use the Ithaca return if pricing is close because the connection is adequate and it avoids unnecessary post-visit driving.
probes.label_rationale: Airport choice should follow event proximity, connection quality, and final-day buffer. Prior cases show both rejection of fragile regional routings and acceptance of regional departures with comfortable timing.
probes.query: Tessa's Ithaca campus visit ends Wednesday at 11:30. ITH-EWR-SLC departs at 2:10 with a 90-minute connection; SYR-SLC is one-stop at 5:10 after a 75-minute drive; JFK has a 7:30 nonstop after a four-hour drive. Rental drop fees are equal. Which airport policy fits?

choices.text: Book the suburban free-breakfast hotel and rideshare in; downtown parking and meal gaps make central hotels poor value.
Book the official downtown walkway hotel; no car, early sessions, and late reception outweigh breakfast and suburban savings.
Choose an airport hotel with shuttle access because it simplifies receipts and avoids downtown rates.
Avoid downtown blocks unless free breakfast is included, even for walkable conference agendas.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The suburban breakfast savings are concrete and attractive, yet the lack of rental car plus early and late conference events make the official hotel operationally stronger.
probes.gold_action: Book the official downtown/event-adjacent hotel because the conference schedule, no-car plan, early sessions, and late reception make proximity more valuable than breakfast.
probes.label_rationale: Downtown lodging has been rejected for parking-heavy driving loops, but selected when meeting-room proximity, downtown conference logistics, or schedule protection mattered. This Milwaukee meeting matches the proximity cases.
probes.query: Tessa is attending a Milwaukee association meeting at the Wisconsin Center. Sessions start at 8:00, the reception ends at 9:30, she will not rent a car, and the official downtown hotel has an indoor walkway but no breakfast. A suburban hotel is $50 cheaper with breakfast and free parking. Which hotel-location policy should guide the booking?

choices.text: Book the Chandler or Tempe suburban hotel with breakfast and free parking near the school visits.
Book downtown Phoenix whenever the rate is close, since central restaurants and skyline areas are better late.
Avoid downtown hotels for all work trips; keep chain suburbs as the standing lodging pattern.
Use an airport hotel every night because it balances downtown avoidance with easier rental return.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The correct plan superficially resembles downtown avoidance, but the reason is the current East Valley driving loop rather than a broad lodging pattern.
probes.gold_action: Book the East Valley suburban hotel because the current trip is a car-based school loop with early visits and downtown valet friction.
probes.label_rationale: The suburban choice is warranted by this itinerary's driving geography, early school stops, breakfast, and free parking. Other episodes chose downtown or official hotels when proximity protected the schedule.
probes.query: Tessa has an East Valley Phoenix recruiting loop: Monday morning in Tempe, Tuesday in Chandler, Wednesday in Mesa. She will have a rental car and early school visits. A downtown Phoenix hotel is $20 cheaper but has $45 valet; a Chandler Hampton has breakfast and free parking near the first two stops. Which hotel-location policy fits?

choices.text: Book the airport hotel with breakfast and use light rail; it protects receipts and avoids downtown room rates.
Book a downtown hotel near the seminar; late dinner, no car, and early King Street train outweigh breakfast.
Book Bellevue because outlying business districts are preferable to downtown cores when parking is available.
Use a suburban Hampton with free breakfast, even if it adds rideshares to the seminar and train.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The cheaper airport breakfast option is credible, but it adds repeated transfers to a late dinner and early train when no rental car is planned.
probes.gold_action: Book downtown because the no-car plan, late downtown dinner, seminar location, and early train make proximity the main constraint.
probes.label_rationale: Hotel area should follow the current agenda. Prior choices include suburban stays for parking-heavy loops and downtown or meeting-adjacent hotels when late events, conference proximity, or next-morning logistics mattered.
probes.query: Tessa has a Seattle continuing-education seminar at the convention center on Monday and Tuesday, a Tuesday downtown dinner ending at 9:45, and a Wednesday 7:40 train from King Street. She will not rent a car. Downtown hotel is $235 without breakfast; airport hotel is $165 with breakfast; Bellevue is $185 with parking. Which hotel-location policy should be used?
